It’s hard to put everything into words, but for at least the past year or so I feel like my mind doesn’t work the way it used to. I’m retired now and live alone, and I spend most days by myself on purpose. I don’t really pick up the phone when friends call anymore; I just don’t have the energy or interest to chat.

What bothers me most is how these memories keep popping into my head out of nowhere. I can be washing dishes or trying to read, and suddenly I’m right back in that moment, like it’s happening again. I can’t seem to push it away, and I keep thinking, “If only I’d done something different, maybe it wouldn’t have happened.” I go over that in my head a lot.

I feel on edge much of the time, like something bad is about to happen. The smallest noise can make me jump, and then my heart races and my hands shake for quite a while before I settle down. My thinking feels sort of foggy—I lose track of what I’m doing, can’t follow the thread of a conversation or a TV show, and it takes me a long time to get myself focused again.
D018-D001_h001.question_a:
It’s been about three years since the car accident, and I still feel like I’m living in it. Out of nowhere, I’ll suddenly see it in my mind, as if it’s happening again—the sound of the crash, my husband slumped over. I don’t want to think about it, but the pictures just come.

Since then I’ve pulled away from people. I used to go to church groups and meet friends for lunch; now I mostly stay home, make excuses not to go out. I keep thinking, “If I’d insisted we leave earlier,” or “If I’d driven instead,” maybe he’d still be here. I go over it again and again, blaming myself.

I feel on edge all the time, like something bad is about to happen. Little things—a door slamming, a car horn—make my heart race and my hands shake, and it takes a long time to settle down. My head feels foggy a lot; I lose track of what I was doing, can’t focus on my books or even follow a TV show. That kind of trouble concentrating really only started after the accident.
D018-D001_h001.question_b:
I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. Teachers used to say I was “bright but away with the fairies.” I couldn’t sit still in class, missed instructions, lost my homework, and at home I’d start chores and then wander off and forget what I was doing. That never really went away. Even before I married, I’d double‑book myself, forget appointments, jump from one thing to another. Now, at 74, I still misplace my glasses three times a day and have trouble following a conversation or a TV plot if anything else is going on. My mind jumps around, and it feels like it’s always been that way.

The trauma came much later, when my husband died suddenly about ten years ago. Since then I sometimes get these sudden, vivid flashes of that night, like it’s replaying. I keep thinking I should have noticed something, that it’s partly my fault. I feel on edge a lot, easily startled, and when something spooks me, my heart races and it takes a long time to settle. I’ve pulled back from friends and church groups, and I spend more time alone than I used to. My head often feels foggy, but the trouble focusing has been there my whole life, long before he died.

I’m not really sure where to start. The main thing is I feel constantly on edge, like my body’s always braced for something. It’s been going on for… a while now, at least months, maybe longer. I get this tightness in my chest and this kind of low-key fear that doesn’t really switch off, even when I’m just sitting at my desk sketching.

Certain sounds or situations just hit me harder than they should. For example, if someone walks up behind me in the office or comes quickly around a corner, I jump way more than seems normal, and my heart just races. Sometimes something small will remind me of what happened, and it’s like my brain locks onto it — I get really upset, almost like I’m back there emotionally, even if I know I’m not.

I’ve also stopped doing a lot of things I used to enjoy. I used to love weekend trips to photograph old buildings, but now I just don’t feel like going anywhere. I keep going over everything in my head, thinking I should’ve handled things differently, that it was partly my fault.

On top of that, my focus is terrible. I misplace my phone, my keys, the project files — I’ll open a drawing set and forget what detail I was supposed to fix. It’s like I’m there physically but my mind keeps slipping away, and I honestly can’t tell if it’s always been this bad or if I’m just noticing it more now.
D018-D001_h002.question_a:

If I hear a loud clang or someone walks up behind me quickly, I jump out of my skin. Even just seeing a building under renovation on the street can set me off—my chest tightens, my mind goes straight back to that day, and I feel this wave of panic that can last for hours.

I’ve pulled back from a lot of things I used to enjoy. I barely sketch for fun anymore, and I stopped going climbing with friends. Most nights I sit at home, just kind of numb but tense at the same time. I keep replaying what happened and thinking, “If I’d double-checked that detail, maybe no one would’ve been hurt.” That thought is constant.

Since the accident I also can’t focus the way I used to. I misplace my keys, forget where I saved project files, reread the same email three times. This wasn’t an issue earlier in my life; it really started only after the accident. And underneath everything there’s this steady, wired fear, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen again.
D018-D001_h002.question_b:

I keep thinking I should’ve seen the other car, that I could’ve prevented it somehow, and that thought just loops. I used to really enjoy sketching for fun or going out with friends, but I don’t feel much interest now. There’s this constant low-level fear and tension sitting in the background.

I’ll reread the same paragraph three times and it still doesn’t stick. I don’t really remember when that started, exactly; it feels like it’s just crept in over time.

Sometimes, especially when I’m alone in certain galleries or in storage, it’s like I’m not fully in the present. I get these episodes where I’m half back in what happened years ago—almost like the room changes, and I’m reacting as if it’s happening again. Physical contact really jolts me when I’m in that state; if a colleague taps my shoulder unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin.

I also notice I’m oddly unmoved by my own accomplishments. A successful opening, a good review—I shrug it off, tell myself anyone could’ve done it. A lot of the time I end up replaying everything and thinking, “If they hadn’t done what they did, none of this would have happened,” and then I spiral into this heavy, embarrassed feeling about the whole thing and about myself, like there’s something fundamentally shameful I can’t shake.
D018-D001_h003.question_a:
It started a little over a year ago, after the break‑in at the museum. Before that, I was meticulous, could spend hours cataloging artifacts without losing focus. Since then, my head feels like it’s full of cotton a lot of the time. I’ll be midway through writing a label and suddenly I just… drift off or can’t hold a thought. That never used to happen.

Sometimes it’s much worse: I’ll hear a loud clang in the storage area, or someone drops a crate, and for a few seconds I’m not in the gallery anymore. I’m back in that night, hearing the glass shatter, feeling my body freeze. It’s so vivid it’s like it’s happening again. If a coworker brushes past me unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin; my whole body tenses before I even realize it’s just a touch.

I used to be proud of my exhibitions, but now I just feel numb about my work. People compliment a show and I think, “It doesn’t matter, I failed when it counted.” I keep replaying the night and blaming security, the board, even myself for not insisting on better protocols. There’s this constant, heavy shame, like I should have prevented everything that happened.

I’m 44 now, but I’ve always been this way. Even in primary school my teachers told my mum I was “bright but scattered” and “never in my seat.” I’d start reading about, say, ancient ceramics and then realize an hour later I’d drifted off, reorganizing my pens or staring out the window. That same restless, jumpy focus has followed me into my job at the museum—I’ll be halfway through writing a catalog entry and suddenly I’m doing three other things and forgot what I was saying.

The trauma stuff came much later. A few years ago I was assaulted walking home. Since then, if someone brushes past me unexpectedly in a gallery, my whole body jolts; I overreact to the slightest touch. Sometimes, especially when I’m shelving objects in the quiet storage rooms, I get these vivid episodes where it feels like I’m back there again—the street, the grip on my arm—so real I lose track of where I am for a moment. My head feels foggy afterwards, like my thoughts are wading through mud.

I used to take pride in my career, but now even getting a new exhibit installed feels hollow. I catch myself thinking none of it really matters, and when colleagues congratulate me, it barely registers. I also can’t shake this sense of humiliation about what happened, like it somehow says something shameful about me, even though I know that’s irrational. Part of me still feels angry and keeps replaying how the police handled it, blaming them for not preventing it, even though another part of me knows that’s not entirely fair.

It’s hard to explain where it all started. I’ve been out here at this station for about three years now, and my head just doesn’t feel right most days. My mind keeps jumping back to what happened on the boat that winter—the storm, the way it all went bad. I’ll be checking the light or logging data and suddenly I’m right back there, like a film I didn’t choose to watch. I try not to talk about that night, and I avoid going near the old dock or even listening to weather reports when they mention storms. I just… steer clear.

Since then, I don’t trust much. Feels like the world’s out to pull you under the moment you let your guard down. Sometimes I catch myself thinking the whole thing was really my supervisor’s fault, or the coast guard’s, that if they’d done their jobs, none of it would’ve happened.

I’m on edge a lot. Small things set me off. Last month I slammed a radio into the wall because it kept cutting out, and I’ve shoved a coworker who startled me from behind. 

My focus is awful—always has been, I think? Or maybe it’s just gotten worse out here. I lose track of checklists, drift off in the middle of readings, have to re-do simple tasks because my mind wanders. It’s like I can’t keep my attention pinned down, whether I’m thinking about the past or just getting through the day.
D018-D001_h013.question_a:
I’ve been out at the lighthouse about six years now, ever since that storm. The night that ship went down… I still see it, over and over, whether I want to or not. I’ll be checking the lamp or trying to sleep and suddenly I’m right back there—waves slamming the rocks, the radio cutting in and out, the flares I couldn’t reach in time. It just forces its way into my head.

Since then I can’t stand anything that reminds me of it. I avoid the cove where the wreck is, won’t go near the old radios or talk to the coast guard guys who were on duty that night. If someone brings it up in town, I just walk out.

My whole view of things has gone sour. I keep thinking the sea, the world in general, is just out to kill you and no one really cares. I blame the port authority, the shipping company, even the supervisor who cut our maintenance budget—I go over what they did wrong and it makes me furious.

I’ve started losing my temper physically. I’ve slammed doors hard enough to crack the frame, thrown tools across the room, once shoved a tech who wouldn’t drop the subject. I never used to be like that.

My concentration went downhill after that storm. Before then I could sit with charts for hours. Now my mind jumps back to that night, I lose my place in the logbook, forget simple steps in the maintenance checklist. It isn’t something I struggled with as a kid; it all started after the wreck.
D018-D001_h013.question_b:
I’ve always been kind of scattered, even as a kid. Teachers used to say I “lived in my own world,” couldn’t sit still, talked over people, and never finished my work. That never really changed. Out here at the lighthouse, I’m constantly losing track of what I’m doing—start checking the generators, then drift off, forget a step, or get pulled into some other task. I misplace tools, leave log entries half done, and my mind jumps around so much I have to reread the same line three, four times.

A few years back there was a bad storm—almost lost a supply boat on the rocks. Since then, I get these flashes of it, like it’s happening again. The sound of the horn in heavy fog, or even the smell of diesel, just slams it back into my head. I go out of my way to avoid talking with the crew from that run or even looking at that part of the coast. I’ve caught myself thinking this whole world is just dangerous and pointless, like what’s the use. I still find myself blaming the company for sending them out in that weather, and when I get wound up, I’ve thrown tools or slammed doors harder than I should.

D018-D001_h022.question_both:
I’ve been struggling for maybe… a couple of years now? It’s hard to pin down exactly when it started. I work as an insurance agent, so I’m on the phone a lot, reading through policies, answering emails, and my mind just slips away. I’ll catch myself rereading the same paragraph three or four times, or zoning out in the middle of a client call and then panicking because I’ve missed what they said. It’s not every day, but enough that my performance reviews have mentioned “focus issues.”

Sleep’s a problem. I get these dreams that feel way too real—same kind of situation over and over, and I wake up with my heart racing and this awful feeling like I’ve done something wrong. I don’t always remember all the details, just the fear and this deep sense of shame that kind of hangs over the next day.

I snap a lot more than I used to—like my daughter spills juice or someone cuts me off in traffic and I just explode, then feel stupid and guilty afterward. Even when something objectively good happens—a bonus at work, a nice weekend away—I feel weirdly flat, like I’m watching someone else enjoy it and I can’t quite access that feeling myself.
D018-D001_h022.question_a:
It started about two years ago, after the car accident. Since then, my sleep hasn’t been the same. I keep having these awful dreams where I’m back in the car—sometimes it’s exactly like it happened, sometimes it’s just the same feeling of terror—but I wake up shaking and soaked in sweat.

Since then I can’t seem to focus the way I used to at work. Before the accident, I could sit with a client, go through a whole policy, remember every detail. Now my mind just blanks or drifts off in the middle of a conversation. It’s not something I struggled with as a kid or earlier in my career; it really started after the crash.

I also walk around feeling…contaminated, I guess. Ashamed. Like I should have done something differently that day. Even when something objectively good happens—my daughter got an award at school, or I close a big account—I feel flat, like I’m watching someone else’s life. And I’ve been snapping over nothing: a coworker misplacing a file, my ex texting late. I go from calm to furious in seconds, then feel stupid and guilty afterward.
D018-D001_h022.question_b:
Honestly, this has been going on as long as I can remember, way before the divorce or anything traumatic. Even in grade school, teachers were always telling my parents I was “bright but unfocused.” I’d miss instructions, lose track mid-sentence, start homework and never finish. That’s pretty much still my life—in my job, I’ll be in the middle of a claim file and suddenly realize I’ve drifted off, or I’ll jump to something else without finishing the first thing. My desk is a mess of half-started things. I interrupt coworkers without meaning to, blurt things out in meetings, and I’ll make these snap decisions I regret, like firing off an angry email over something minor.

Since the accident a few years ago, I’ve also been having these awful, repeating dreams about it. I wake up feeling this deep shame, like it was somehow my fault, and I can’t shake that feeling during the day. Even when something good happens—like my daughter doing well in school or getting a bonus at work—I feel flat, like I’m watching it from the outside. And the anger… it’s like I go from zero to yelling over something tiny, then feel horrible afterward.

D018-D001_h023.question_both:
I work as a social media manager, so I’m online all the time, and it feels like my brain just doesn’t switch off anymore. For about… I don’t know, months now, maybe longer, I’ve been on edge all the time. The smallest thing sets me off—someone changing a brief last minute, a notification sound—I snap or feel like I’m going to.

Sometimes it’s like I’m not really in the room. I’ll be scheduling posts and suddenly I’m back in that situation from a few years ago, like it’s happening again. I can see it and feel it, and for a few seconds I forget where I actually am. It’s like I’m watching it through my own eyes again, not just remembering.

I can’t shake this constant feeling that what happened was somehow my fault. Even when people tell me it wasn’t, I keep replaying what I could’ve done differently. And even when good things happen—a campaign does really well, I get positive feedback—I just feel… flat. I know I “should” be happy, but it doesn’t land.

On top of that, focusing is really hard. My mind jumps around during meetings, I miss details in briefs, and I reread the same email three times before it sticks. I’m not even sure when that started; it just feels like my attention slips away really easily now.
D018-D001_h023.question_a:
It all really started after what happened last summer. Before that, I could juggle six campaigns at once, plan content calendars for weeks, no problem. Since then, my brain just… doesn’t lock in. I’ll open a dashboard to schedule posts and suddenly I’m staring at the screen, rereading the same line over and over. It wasn’t like this growing up; in school and in my first job I could focus fine. This is new, and it came after the incident.

The worst part is when something random triggers it—a sound, a smell, a certain angle of light—and it’s like I’m yanked out of the room. I’m not just remembering; I’m back there. I can feel my body freeze, my heart racing, and for those moments it’s like the whole thing is happening again.

Since then I’m on edge all the time. Tiny things set me off—coworkers asking simple questions, my phone buzzing—and I snap or feel this surge of anger I can’t control. Even when good things happen, like a campaign doing really well or friends inviting me out, it’s like there’s a wall. I can’t feel happy, and honestly, I don’t think I deserve to, because I keep thinking I should’ve done something different that day. The guilt just never shuts up.
D018-D001_h023.question_b:
I’ve always been kind of “all over the place,” even as a kid. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was smart but never finished what I started, constantly daydreaming or blurting things out. I remember in elementary school I’d start my homework, then get up, forget what I was doing, start something else. That scattered, restless feeling has pretty much been there my whole life.

Now, with my job running multiple social media accounts, it’s a mess. I’ll open my laptop to schedule posts, then end up scrolling, jumping between tabs, forgetting deadlines. My mind jumps so fast I lose track mid-sentence, and I’m fidgety in meetings, interrupting people without meaning to.

On top of that, after what happened last year—the assault—I keep getting these episodes where it’s like I’m back there. I zone out and suddenly my body feels like it’s reliving it; it’s not just a memory. Since then, I feel constantly on edge and snappy over tiny things. My friends say I “go off” over nothing. I also carry this heavy guilt, like somehow it was my fault, and even when something good happens at work or in my life, it’s like I’m numb—I can’t actually feel happy.

D018-D001_h024.question_a:

Before that, yeah, I could get distracted sometimes, but I could focus on jobs fine—doing designs, planning out a whole garden in my head, no problem. Since the crash, it’s like my brain just… slips. I’ll be standing there with the hedge trimmer in my hand, totally blank, can’t remember what I was doing, or I’ll zone out staring at a flower bed and lose whole chunks of time.

Sometimes it’s worse than zoning out. I’m back there—smell of burning rubber, glass hitting my face. I’m not in the garden anymore; I’m in the car, braced for the impact. I’ve dropped tools because of it.

I can’t shake this feeling that it was somehow my fault, that I should’ve done something different that night. Every day I’m replaying it, thinking I don’t deserve to feel good. Even when a client loves my work or my mates invite me out, it’s like there’s this wall—I just can’t feel happy, just numb.

And I snap over nothing now. Someone misplaces a rake or bumps into me, and I just explode, proper shouting, then feel awful straight after.

It’s been… I’m not even sure, a few years at least, that things have felt off. Since my wife passed it’s gotten more noticeable, or maybe I just don’t have anyone to smooth things over anymore.

Little things set me off. If someone surprises me from behind in the supermarket, or if there’s a certain kind of shouting on the TV, my heart starts pounding, my hands sweat, and I feel like I have to get out of there right away. I don’t always understand why that particular sound or situation does it, but my body reacts before my head catches up.

I’m ashamed a lot of the time, like there’s something rotten about me that I can’t wash off, especially when I think back on things I went through earlier in life. I don’t talk about it; I just feel… dirty, I guess. And then other times I feel nothing at all, like someone turned the volume down on my emotions. The grandkids come over and I know I should feel happy, but it’s like I’m watching it from behind glass.

I also lose track of what I’m doing very easily now. I’ll start a task and drift off, or halfway through a conversation I realize I’ve missed what the other person was saying. That makes me snap sometimes—I raise my voice, bark at the kids on the phone, or bite the nurse’s head off for small things. I hear myself shouting and blaming, but it’s like I can’t put the brakes on until it’s already done.
D018-D001_h025.question_a:
It really started after my wife died two years ago. She had a sudden heart attack right in front of me at home. Ever since then, my mind hasn’t worked the same.

If anything reminds me of that night—the sound of an ambulance on TV, the beeping in the hospital when I go for my checkups—my body just goes haywire. My heart starts pounding, my hands shake, I get sweaty and short of breath, like I’m right back in that living room watching her go. Sometimes it’s just a thought that pops into my head, and I feel it in my chest immediately.

I used to be a pretty even-tempered guy, but now I snap at people over nothing. My son calls to check in and I end up shouting at him, or I bite the nurse’s head off if she’s a few minutes late. I hear myself cursing and blaming them and then feel awful afterward.

Most days I feel…blank. It’s like everything inside is shut off. Things I used to enjoy—reading the newspaper, chatting with neighbors—don’t bring anything up, good or bad. Just emptiness, and this constant sense that what happened to my wife was somehow my fault. I keep thinking I should have noticed something, done something. That shame just sits there.

And since that night, I can’t focus the way I used to. I lose track of what I’m reading, forget what I was about to do, get stuck in the middle of a sentence. I never had that kind of trouble when I was younger or working; it’s only been since all this happened.

I’m here because things have been getting harder to manage, but it’s not really new. My mind has always jumped around. Even as a kid, before middle school, teachers said I “never stayed in my seat” and my report cards always said “easily distracted, doesn’t finish work.” I’d start one thing, then another, and forget what I was doing. That never really went away, even through my working years and now in retirement—I'll go to pay a bill or make tea and end up wandering off, leaving things half-done.

Since my wife died and that fall I had a few years back, certain noises or sudden movements set me off physically—my heart pounds, my chest tightens, I feel sweaty and shaky. I also carry this constant sense of disgrace about needing help, like I failed somehow, and it’s hard to shake. At the same time, I feel strangely hollow a lot of the time, like I’m going through the motions, not really feeling joy, even with my grandkids. When I do get overwhelmed, I can snap and start yelling or cursing at my son over small things, then feel awful about it afterward.
